plates.title: Most rural households own land; deposits are close to universal
plates.sub: Households reporting each kind of asset, per 1,000 households.
plates.explain: One household can own several kinds of asset, so these rates do not add up. A household counts as owning land or a building whatever its value.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 77 All India Debt and Investment Survey

plates.title: Land and buildings carry most of the value
plates.sub: Average value per household, in rupees, across all households including those without the asset.
plates.explain: These averages include households that own none of the asset, so the figure for shares is small even though the households that hold shares may hold a lot. Gold and jewellery are counted separately, in the next chart.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 77 All India Debt and Investment Survey

plates.title: Gold and jewellery sit outside the asset total
plates.sub: Households reporting gold, silver or jewellery, per 1,000 households.
plates.explain: The survey records bullion and ornaments apart from its total of physical and financial assets, so they are not part of the average asset values above.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 77 All India Debt and Investment Survey

plates.title: Assets climb steeply up the ladder
plates.sub: Average assets per household in each tenth of households, ranked by assets, rural and urban ranked separately.
plates.explain: Each decile is a tenth of rural (or urban) households, ranked from the poorest in assets to the richest. The top decile’s average shows how much of the total sits with a few households.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 77 All India Debt and Investment Survey

plates.title: Assets differ across social groups
plates.sub: Average assets per household by social group, in rupees.
plates.explain: An average says nothing about the spread inside a group: some households in every group own far more than its average, and many own far less.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 77 All India Debt and Investment Survey

plates.title: Livelihood shapes what a household owns
plates.sub: Average assets per household by the household’s main source of income, in rupees.
plates.explain: The survey classifies a household by its main livelihood. Rural and urban households use different classes, so compare within a sector.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 77 All India Debt and Investment Survey

plates.title: Households headed by women own less
plates.sub: Average assets per household by the sex of the household head, in rupees.
plates.explain: This classifies the household by its head. It does not say what women own in their own name.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 77 All India Debt and Investment Survey

plates.title: Rural assets vary widely across states
plates.sub: Average assets per rural household in each state and union territory, in rupees.
plates.explain: State estimates rest on smaller samples than the all-India figure, and the survey uses the state boundaries of 2018. Urban estimates for every state are in Every Cut below.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 77 All India Debt and Investment Survey

plates.title: Households with more assets borrow more often
plates.sub: Households with an outstanding cash loan per 1,000 households, by asset decile.
plates.explain: A household counts once however many loans it has. Deciles rank households by assets, as in the chart of asset values.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 77 All India Debt and Investment Survey
plates.group: What households owe, and to whom

plates.title: The debt of a borrowing household is far higher than the average
plates.sub: Average cash debt per indebted household, in rupees, as published by MoSPI.
plates.explain: The headline average debt divides by every household, including the many with no loan. This chart divides only by households that owe money, which is the figure a borrowing family would recognise.
plates.source: MoSPI, AIDIS release published by PIB
plates.group: What households owe, and to whom

plates.title: Banks hold most household debt; in villages, moneylenders still hold a large share
plates.sub: Of every ₹1,000 households owe, how much is owed to each kind of lender.
plates.explain: These shares divide the money owed, not the households. Insurance companies, provident funds, employers, financial corporations, chit funds, traders and SHGs not linked to banks hold the rest; they are in Every Cut.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 77 All India Debt and Investment Survey
plates.group: What households owe, and to whom

plates.title: Most household debt costs between 6 and 15 per cent a year
plates.sub: Of every ₹1,000 owed, how much carries each annual rate of interest.
plates.explain: The bands are the annual rate of interest on each loan. Interest-free loans are in Every Cut, by lender.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.

plates.title: What the money was borrowed for
plates.sub: Of every ₹1,000 owed, how much was borrowed for each purpose.
plates.explain: The purpose is the use the household reported when the loan was taken. Farm and business borrowing is split into investment and running costs.
plates.vintageNote: The archived AIDIS API rows contain no publisher revision timestamp. The survey report was released on 2021-09-10, but the current API body has not been established as that exact publication version.

plates.title: How common borrowing is, state by state
plates.sub: Rural households with an outstanding cash loan per 1,000 households, by state.
plates.explain: State estimates rest on smaller samples than the all-India figure. Urban estimates are in Every Cut below.

plates.title: Housing takes most of what households invest
plates.sub: Average spending per household on new fixed assets over the year, in rupees, across all households.
plates.explain: This is spending on building or buying fixed assets during the year to June 2019, not the stock of assets. Most households spent nothing, which keeps these averages low.
